Variableness
VAIR-i-a-bl-ness
n. (changeableness; liability to alter)
Greek parallage, a change or variation — the word from which the English parallax descends, used of the shifting of a heavenly body's apparent position. James pairs it with shadow of turning, and both terms are drawn from the movement of lights across the sky.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. The imagery is astronomical, and it is chosen with care. James calls God the Father of lights — the maker of sun, moon, and stars. Every one of those lights varies. The sun climbs and declines and casts a shadow that moves all day; the moon waxes and wanes; the stars wheel and set. Having named God as their Father, James then says the one thing that is not true of any of them: with him is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. The lights change; the One who made them does not. The doctrinal weight is the divine immutability, and James introduces it for an intensely practical reason. He has just warned that no man may say he is tempted of God, and he is establishing why the character of God can be relied upon absolutely: God does not have moods, phases, or a dark side that comes round in its season. What comes down from him is every good gift and every perfect gift, without exception and without alternation. The Scriptures say the same in plainer words: I am the LORD, I change not; and, God is not a man, that he should lie; and of the Son, Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): susceptibility of change; liableness or aptness to alter; changeableness; inconstancy.

expand to see more

VARIABLENESS, n. Susceptibility of change; liableness or aptness to alter.

VARIABLENESS, n. Changeableness; inconstancy; instability; levity; fickleness.

VARIABLE, a. That may vary or alter; changeable; mutable; that may be altered.

IMMUTABLE, a. Unchangeable; unalterable; that cannot be altered or changed.

SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane and representing the form of the body which intercepts the rays of light.

Key Scripture

James 1:17 — "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."

Malachi 3:6 — "For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed."

Numbers 23:19 — "God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?"

Hebrews 13:8 — "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever."

Modern Corruption

Divine immutability is denied outright by process theology and qualified into insignificance by open theism; James asserts it as the ground of every good gift and of the believer's confidence in God's character.

expand to see more

Process theology denies divine immutability by construction, making God a being who develops with the world; open theism, following Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders, denies exhaustive foreknowledge and so makes God a learner who adjusts as the future arrives. Both are errors, and both are answered here. James does not say God is reliable in the main, or unchanging in his essential character while variable in knowledge and purpose. He says no variableness and neither shadow of turning, using the language of celestial motion precisely in order to exclude even the slightest shift. Malachi grounds Israel's survival on the same fact: I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.

A common objection holds that immutability is a Greek philosophical intrusion, unable to account for the texts where God is said to repent. The Reformed answer is old and sound. Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 state the doctrine flatly in the same canon that contains those texts, which means Scripture does not regard them as contradictory; the language of divine repentance describes God's unchanging purpose meeting changed creatures, not a change in God. Immutability is not divine coldness. It is the reason a believer's worst day does not find God in a different mood, and why what comes down from the Father of lights is good, and perfect, and does not alternate.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parallage (G3883), variation or change; trope (G5157), a turning; aposkiasma (G644), a shadow cast; dosis (G1394), a giving or gift.

expand to see more

Greek parallage (G3883) — variation, the shifting of a light's position; rendered variableness, its only occurrence.

Greek trope (G5157) — a turning, as of the solstice; rendered turning, its only occurrence.

Greek aposkiasma (G644) — a shadow cast by something turning; rendered shadow, its only occurrence.

Greek dosis (G1394) — the act of giving, a gift; every one of them from above.

Hebrew shanah (H8138) — to change, to alter; denied of the LORD at Malachi 3:6.

Usage

"“with whom is no variableness” — immutability, stated of the Father of lights."

"“neither shadow of turning” — no phase, no declining, no dark side."

"“I am the LORD, I change not” — the same doctrine in the prophets."
